assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Use strong induction on n. For n=2 the claim is immediate. For n>=3, fix any sign sequence s. Split counted permutations by the position p of the maximum value n; this gives the recurrence of L1. The left and right parts are smaller sign-pattern problems, so the induction hypothesis bounds each term by the corresponding alternating maxima M_{p-1} and M_{n-p}. This yields an upper bound by a weighted sum over Peak(s). By L2, Peak(s) is a subset with no adjacent elements. The bottleneck lemma L5 says that among all such subsets, the weighted sum is maximized exactly by one entire parity class. L4 identifies each parity-class sum with M_n, the count of an alternating pattern. Hence every sign sequence satisfies F_n(s) <= M_n, while the two alternating patterns both achieve M_n by definition and the symmetry L3. Finally, if some s is maximizing, then every inequality in the upper-bound chain is tight; the equality clause in L5 forces Peak(s) to be a full parity class, and L6 reconstructs s as one of the two alternating sign sequences. Therefore the maximizing sign sequences are exactly the alternating ones.

steps.derives: Base case n=2: the only length-1 sign sequences are (+1) and (-1), each has count 1, so both are maximal and both are alternating.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the explicit base-case computation supplied by L7.

steps.derives: Induction setup for n >= 3: assume as strong induction hypothesis that for every integer m with 2 <= m < n and every sign sequence u of length m-1, one has F_m(u) <= M_m, and equality holds only for the two alternating sign sequences alt_m^+ and alt_m^-. Also note separately that F_0(empty)=M_0=1 and F_1(empty)=M_1=1 by definition.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the standard strong induction assumption specialized to the statement being proved.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary sign sequence s of length n-1. Applying the recurrence by the position of the value n gives F_n(s)=sum_{p in Peak(s)} binomial(n-1,p-1) F_{p-1}(s^{<p}) F_{n-p}(s^{>p}).
steps.trivial_justification: L1 is applied with m=n and t=s.

steps.derives: For each p in Peak(s), the factors F_{p-1}(s^{<p}) and F_{n-p}(s^{>p}) involve sizes strictly smaller than n. If one factor has size 0 or 1, it equals M_0 or M_1 by definition; otherwise it is at most the corresponding M-value by the strong induction hypothesis from A2. Therefore each summand in A3 is at most w_p^(n)=binomial(n-1,p-1) M_{p-1} M_{n-p}, and summing over p yields F_n(s) <= sum_{p in Peak(s)} w_p^(n).
steps.trivial_justification: This step combines the recurrence from A3 with the strong induction hypothesis for the smaller left and right subproblems.

steps.derives: The set Peak(s) has no consecutive integers.
steps.trivial_justification: Immediate from L2 applied to the fixed sign sequence s.

steps.derives: Because Peak(s) is a subset of {1,...,n} with no consecutive integers, the weighted independent-set inequality applies and gives sum_{p in Peak(s)} w_p^(n) <= max(sum_{1 <= p <= n, p even} w_p^(n), sum_{1 <= p <= n, p odd} w_p^(n)).
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly L5 with m=n and P=Peak(s).

steps.derives: For the same weights w_p^(n), the maximum of the even-parity sum and the odd-parity sum is M_n, because L4 states that both parity sums are equal to M_n.
steps.trivial_justification: Direct application of L4 with m=n.

steps.derives: Combining A4 and A6 gives F_n(s) <= max(sum_{p even} w_p^(n), sum_{p odd} w_p^(n)).
steps.trivial_justification: This is a single transitive comparison of the inequalities already obtained.

steps.derives: Substituting the value of the parity maximum from A7 into the inequality from A8 yields F_n(s) <= M_n for every sign sequence s of length n-1.
steps.trivial_justification: A8 gives an upper bound by the parity maximum, and A7 identifies that parity maximum with M_n.

steps.derives: By definition, F_n(alt_n^+)=M_n. By L3, negating the sign pattern preserves the count, so F_n(alt_n^-)=F_n(alt_n^+)=M_n. Thus both alternating sign sequences attain the upper bound M_n.
steps.trivial_justification: This step uses the definition of M_n together with the symmetry from L3 to get both alternating witnesses.

steps.derives: Therefore the maximal value of F_n among all sign sequences of length n-1 is exactly M_n, and both alternating sign sequences are maximizing.
steps.trivial_justification: A9 gives the universal upper bound M_n, and A10 provides sign sequences that attain it.

steps.derives: Now assume s is any maximizing sign sequence of length n-1. Since the maximal value is M_n by A11, we have F_n(s)=M_n.
steps.trivial_justification: A maximizing sequence must attain the maximum value identified in A11.

steps.derives: From A4, A6, and A7 we have a chain F_n(s) <= sum_{p in Peak(s)} w_p^(n) <= M_n. Because A12 says the left endpoint already equals M_n, both inequalities in that chain are equalities. In particular, equality holds in the L5 inequality used in A6, so the equality clause of L5 forces Peak(s) to be exactly the even integers in {1,...,n} or exactly the odd integers in {1,...,n}.
steps.trivial_justification: This step extracts the equality information from the sharp upper-bound chain and then invokes the equality characterization in L5.

steps.derives: If Peak(s) is the even set, then L6 gives s=alt_n^+. If Peak(s) is the odd set, then L6 gives s=alt_n^-. Hence every maximizing sign sequence is alternating.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the reconstruction statement of L6 applied to the two peak-set possibilities from A13.

steps.derives: The base case A1 handles n=2. For arbitrary n >= 3, steps A11 and A14 prove the induction step: among all sign sequences s=(s_1,...,s_{n-1}) with each s_i=±1, the quantity f(s)=F_n(s) is maximal exactly for the alternating sequences s=(+1,-1,+1,-1,...) and s=(-1,+1,-1,+1,...), equivalently exactly for those s satisfying s_i s_{i+1}=-1 for every 1 <= i <= n-2. This is exactly the theorem statement.
steps.trivial_justification: This closes the strong induction by combining the base case with the full induction step and then rewriting F_n as the theorem's f.

lemmas.statement_nl:
Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let t=(t_1,...,t_{m-1}) be a sign sequence with each t_i in {+1,-1}. Let F_m(t) be the number of permutations a=(a_1,...,a_m) of {1,...,m} such that t_i(a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0 for every 1 <= i <= m-1. Define Peak(t) subseteq {1,...,m} by: 1 in Peak(t) iff t_1=-1; m in Peak(t) iff t_{m-1}=+1; and for 2 <= p <= m-1, p in Peak(t) iff t_{p-1}=+1 and t_p=-1. For p in Peak(t), define t^{<p}=(t_1,...,t_{p-2}) with the convention that this is the empty sequence when p <= 2, and define t^{>p}=(t_{p+1},...,t_{m-1}) with the convention that this is the empty sequence when p >= m-1. Then, with F_0(empty)=F_1(empty)=1, one has
F_m(t) = sum over p in Peak(t) of binomial(m-1,p-1) * F_{p-1}(t^{<p}) * F_{m-p}(t^{>p}).
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: It is a structural recurrence for one fixed sign pattern; it does not compare different patterns or identify maximizers.

full_candidate.strategy_summary: Strong induction on n using the position of the maximum entry. A recurrence expresses the count for an arbitrary sign pattern as a sum over the positions where the value n can occur. After replacing the smaller factors by the corresponding alternating-pattern maxima, the problem becomes a weighted independent-set problem on the path {1,...,n}. A bottleneck lemma says those Euler-type weights are maximized exactly by one full parity class of vertices, and those parity classes correspond exactly to the two alternating sign sequences.

payload.theorem_nl: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \\geq 2$. For a sequence $s = (s_1,\\dots,s_{n-1})$ where each $s_i = \\pm 1$, let $f(s)$ be the number of permutations $(a_1,\\dots,a_n)$ of $\\{1,2,\\dots,n\\}$ such that $s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0$ for all $i$. For each $n$, determine the sequences $s$ for which $f(s)$ is maximal.

steps.derives: For any such maximizing s, the earlier bounds still give the chain F_n(s) <= sum over p in Peak(s) of w_p^(n) <= max( sum of w_p^(n) over even p in {1,...,n}, sum of w_p^(n) over odd p in {1,...,n} ).
steps.trivial_justification: This is just A4 and A6 written together as one inequality chain.

steps.derives: Replacing the parity maximum in A13 by M_n using A7 yields F_n(s) <= sum over p in Peak(s) of w_p^(n) <= M_n.
steps.trivial_justification: A7 identifies the right-hand endpoint of the chain in A13.

steps.derives: Because A12 says F_n(s) = M_n and A14 places sum over p in Peak(s) of w_p^(n) between F_n(s) and M_n, both inequalities in A14 are equalities. Hence sum over p in Peak(s) of w_p^(n) = M_n, and since A7 also identifies M_n with the parity maximum, we get sum over p in Peak(s) of w_p^(n) = max( sum of w_p^(n) over even p in {1,...,n}, sum of w_p^(n) over odd p in {1,...,n} ).
steps.trivial_justification: Equality at the two endpoints of the chain forces equality in the middle, and A7 rewrites that common value as the parity maximum.

steps.derives: The equality clause in L5 now applies to P = Peak(s), so Peak(s) is exactly the set of even integers in {1,...,n} or exactly the set of odd integers in {1,...,n}.
steps.trivial_justification: A5 gives the no-consecutive hypothesis required by L5, and A15 gives the equality hypothesis.

steps.derives: If Peak(s) is the even set then s = alt_n^+, and if Peak(s) is the odd set then s = alt_n^-. Therefore every maximizing sign sequence is alternating.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the reconstruction statement of L6 applied to the two possibilities from A16.

steps.derives: Under the strong induction hypothesis A2, we have proved the full induction step for this fixed n >= 3: among all sign sequences of length n-1, the count F_n is maximized exactly by the two alternating sign sequences.
steps.trivial_justification: A11 gives the exact maximum value and the existence of alternating maximizers, while A17 gives uniqueness of the maximizing patterns.

steps.derives: Let n be an integer with n >= 2. For a sequence s = (s_1,...,s_{n-1}) where each s_i = ±1, let f(s) be the number of permutations (a_1,...,a_n) of {1,2,...,n} such that s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0 for all i. Then f(s) is maximal exactly for the two alternating sequences s = (+1,-1,+1,-1,...) and s = (-1,+1,-1,+1,...), equivalently exactly for those s satisfying s_i s_{i+1} = -1 for every 1 <= i <= n-2.
steps.trivial_justification: A1 establishes the base case n = 2, A18 supplies the induction step for every n >= 3, and strong induction yields the theorem for all n >= 2. The theorem's function f is the same counting function denoted F_n in the auxiliary notation.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let t = (t_1,...,t_{m-1}) be a sign sequence with each t_i in {+1,-1}. Define F_m(t) to be the number of permutations a = (a_1,...,a_m) of {1,...,m} such that t_i (a_{i+1} - a_i) > 0 for every 1 <= i <= m-1. Define Peak(t) as the subset of {1,...,m} given by: 1 is in Peak(t) iff t_1 = -1; m is in Peak(t) iff t_{m-1} = +1; and for 2 <= p <= m-1, p is in Peak(t) iff t_{p-1} = +1 and t_p = -1. For each integer p with 1 <= p <= m, define t^{<p} = (t_1,...,t_{p-2}) with the convention that this is the empty sequence when p <= 2, and define t^{>p} = (t_{p+1},...,t_{m-1}) with the convention that this is the empty sequence when p >= m-1. Set F_0(empty) = 1 and F_1(empty) = 1. Then F_m(t) = sum over p in Peak(t) of binomial(m-1, p-1) * F_{p-1}(t^{<p}) * F_{m-p}(t^{>p}).
lemmas.strictly_easier_reason: It is a decomposition formula for one fixed sign pattern and does not compare different patterns or identify maximizers.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let t = (t_1,...,t_{m-1}) be a sign sequence with each t_i in {+1,-1}. Define Peak(t) as the subset of {1,...,m} given by: 1 is in Peak(t) iff t_1 = -1; m is in Peak(t) iff t_{m-1} = +1; and for 2 <= p <= m-1, p is in Peak(t) iff t_{p-1} = +1 and t_p = -1. If Peak(t) is exactly the set of even integers in {1,...,m}, then t_i = +1 for odd i and t_i = -1 for even i, so t is the alternating sequence (+1,-1,+1,-1,...). If Peak(t) is exactly the set of odd integers in {1,...,m}, then t_i = -1 for odd i and t_i = +1 for even i, so t is the alternating sequence (-1,+1,-1,+1,...).
